sn22.22:1.2: This discourse is much-quoted in later texts of both Pali and Sanskrit Buddhism, especially in discussions trying to resolve the question of what the Buddha meant by “person” (_puggala_). One school of Buddhism, the Pudgalavādins, argued that the “person” was as real as anything else, even if it could not be well defined, a position that was thoroughly rejected by other schools, including the Theravada ([kv1.1]()). The text itself uses a subtle complex of imagery to make its point.
sn22.22:1.5: The basic meaning of _khandha (Sanskrit _skandha_) is “trunk” of a tree (Rig Veda 1.32.5, Atharva Veda 10.7.38) or a person (= “shoulders”, Atharva Veda 6.25.2, 6.135.1, etc.). Thus the aggregates themselves can be considered what “shoulders” the burden (like buffaloes, Arthaśāstra 2.29.8).  the three _dharmaskandha_ (“trunks of religious duty”, Chandogya Upaniṣad 2.23.1). For the Jains, the _skandha_ was a type of matter (_pudgala_) consisting of two or more combined “atoms” (_aṇu_), namely a “molecule” (Tattvārthasūtra 5.5).
sn22.22:2.2: The etymology of _puggala_ (Sanskrit _pudgala_) is unclear, but it is a primarily Buddhist and Jain term, being absent from pre-Buddhist texts. Pali is rich in terms for a “person” (_purisa_, _jana_, _jantu_, _nara_, _manussa_), raising the question why _puggala_ is used. _Puggala_ is the normal term used especially in the Aṅguttara Nikāya when describing certain “individuals” and their characteristics; these are collected in the Abhidhamma book the Puggalapaññatti. The Jain meaning of _pudgala_ is “mass”, “matter” (Tattvārthasūtra 5.5). That this sense is not peculiar to the Jains is shown by its use for a “mass” (of gold) by Kauṭilya (Arthaśastra 2.14.7, 2.14.43). In this way the word _puggala_ connects with the idea of _khandha_ as an “aggregate”, “bundle”. Perhaps the Buddha favored this term because it avoided Vedic terminology, while at the same time suggesting a connection with the _khandha_ doctrine that the “person” comprised a “mass” of components. Try reading this Sutta and substituting “mass” for “person”.
